messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: censoring w/o cumulative densities
parts:
We can use Stan's constrained variables if we sample latent
parameters corresponding to censored measurements:

data {
double C;

int(0,) N_c;
double x_c[N_c];

int(0,) N_uc;
double x_uc[N_uc];
double(,C) y_uc[N_uc];
...
}
parameters {
double(C,) y_c[N_c];
...
}
model {
for (n in 1:N_c)
y_c[n] ~ normal(alpha * x_c[n] + beta, sigma);

for (n in 1:N_uc)
y_uc[n] ~ normal(alpha * x_uc[n] + beta, sigma);
...
}

The uncensored data is already in the proper range (the
ranges on the data are just for error checking the data
input).

The declaration double(C,) for the censored data vector y_c
forces each y_c[n] to be sampled from the range (C,inf).

The version using the cumulative density removes the
parameter y_c and replaces its sampling loop with:

for (n in 1:N_c)
1 ~ bernoulli(c_normal_lb(alpha * x_c[n] + beta, sigma, C));

This formulation effectively integrates out the parameter
vector y_c.

- Bob

parts:
More generally, we need left censored, right censored, and interval censored:
data {
   double(C, )  y_rc[n_lc];
   double(, C)  y_lc[n_rc];
   double(C1, C2)  y_lrc[n_lrc];
}

And C might be a vector: different censoring mechanism for each data point.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] censoring w/o cumulative densities
parts:
On 12/5/11 8:17 PM, Jiqiang Guo wrote:
> More generally, we need left censored, right censored, and interval
> censored:

Exactly.

Right now, you can bound double parameters above, below, or
both and they'll be appropriately transformed (log, log,
logit). You can also bound double data this way, but that
only comes into the compiled code as an error check.
There are also more complex multivariate bounds for simplexes,
ordered positive values (for ordered logit bounds) and
covariance and correlation matrices. There are a bunch of
classes in stan::io for this and the unit tests and doc
show how it'll work and provide all the definitions of
the transform, and its log Jacobian determinant.

What we haven't implemented are all the truncated
densities (left, right, both) and all the
cumulative density functions (left, right, both again).
And ideally those'd also get pre-built derivatives.
There's a lot of spade-work left to do building this out
and even more if we want the gradients and proportionality
to be calculated efficiently.

At around 15 distributions total, that'll be
7 variations, each with 2 forms due to error propagation,
for a total of around 210 functions to write. Each of those
should then get a class to efficiently implement its
gradients. Makes me tired just thinking about it.

Which ones are the most important for models? We'll
at least have to do all the ones for the BUGS models.

> And C might be a vector: different censoring mechanism
> for each data point.

If there's a different set of lower and upper bound
censoring for each point, we're not going to be able
to declare that as part of the variable definition and
use the simple latent variable method -- we'll have
to evaluate the truncated distributions.

If the bounds are variable, it's even trickier, but
with the cumulatives, it can still be worked out, I think.

Sounds like you'd like to help write the manual!
That's up next.

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: censoring w/o cumulative densities
parts:
This old thread pertains to my question in the other thread about
missing data, here in the case of censoring ...

On Dec 5 2011, 10:25 pm, Bob Carpenter <c...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> If there's a different set of lower and upper bound censoring for each point, we're not going to be able
> to declare that as part of the variable definition and
> use the simple latent variable method -- we'll have
> to evaluate the truncated distributions.

Is there a fundamental problem with writing out a censored vector of
length n_lc as a set of n_lc scalars to utilize the "simple latent
variable method" when the CDF method is not available or practical?

Say a human wants to write this

data {
int(0,) n_lc;
double C[n_lc];
double(C, ) y_rc[n_lc];
}
...
model {
for(i in 1:n_lc) y_rc[i] ~ normal(mu[i], sigma);
}

so C is some long vector of censoring points. But instead writes
(possible aided by some script)

data {
int(0,) n_lc;
# unvector the C-vector to n_lc scalars
double(42.0, ) __y_rc_1;
double(17.6, ) __y_rc_2;
...
double(32.8, ) __y_rc_n_lc;
}
...
model {
# unroll the for loop
__y_rc_1 ~ normal(mu[1], sigma);
__y_rc_2 ~ normal(mu[2], sigma);
...
__y_rc_n_lc ~ normal(mu[n_lc], sigma);
}

That is obviously ugly and unrolling the loops is going to slow things
down, but if the CDF is not available in closed form, auto-diffing it
is going to also be slow.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: censoring w/o cumulative densities
parts:
The unrolled version is perfectly legal,
but I don't understand what the issue is with
either model.

The bounds on the data don't do anything -- they're
just there for error checking on data read.

Unrolling won't slow things down noticeably (nor will
it likely speed things up because of cache issues).
All of the index and array and loop work is completely
dominated by the logs and auto-dif.

The cumulative densities and their derivatives
can be expensive. We might not be able to compute
them in some cases due to memory issues if some
iterative algorithm is too intense. Auto-dif uses
a minimum of 24 bytes for each operation on
parameters executed in an algorithm.

The only reason for the __ in the generated
code was light name mangling to avoid clashing
with user variables, which by fiat can't end
in "__".

I take it by this:

> double C[n_lc];
> double(C, ) y_rc[n_lc];

you meant that each parameter had a different bound.
Note legal in Stan as is, but it's an intriguing
possibility. I've been thinking more about vectorizing
notation, but hadn't thought about this kind of usage.

In most cases, we won't need to compute the
cumulative density anyway. For instance, if
we have censoring, neither the uncensored data
nor the censored data needs to draw from truncated
distributions. Suppose z[1:N] are the censored points
and y[1:M] have values below the censoring bound
alpha, then we'd have:

data {
int(0,) M;
int(0,) N;
double alpha;
double(,alpha) y[M];
parameters {
double(alpha,0) z[N];
double mu;
double(0,) sigma;
}
model {
for (m in 1:M)
y[M] ~ normal(mu,sigma);
for (n in 1:N)
z[N] ~ normal(mu,sigma);
mu ~ ...
sigma ~ ...
}

Now if alpha's not known, it's a different matter.
Though we can still transform so that we don't have
to compute cumulative densities.

I've really got to write the manual!

- Bob
